entries.value: Junior astronaut training at Base ARES
Move with WASD or the arrow keys. On a phone, drag the joystick.
Walk to a glowing station and press USE (E or Space).
Follow the yellow arrow to your next stop.
Bubble will tell you what each room does!
Crew radiation dose: 0–100 game units, not real dose. Mars lacks a thick atmosphere and global magnetic field to block particles.
Triangles rendered per frame, including rendering passes
Integrity and Oxygen starting values and damage are provisional game rules. The Energy bar shows how much of today's need your plan covers.
Hi, I'm Bubble! Welcome to Base ARES on Mars. Follow the yellow arrow!
The Control Room is the heart of the base. We plan every Sol from here.
The Weather Station watches wind, temperature and pressure on Mars.
In the Laboratory we study rocks and dust. Science time!
Plants grow here. Look, they get bigger every Sol!
Life Support keeps our air fresh so we can breathe.
Communications sends messages all the way to Earth. Hi, Earth!
The Magnetic Shield refuge has thick walls. We hide here during solar storms.
From the Observatory we watch the Sun and the sky.
The Airlock is the door to the outside. Suits on before going out!
The Magnetic Shield protects the base. Its reinforced refuge keeps the crew safe.
The solar panels supply our game energy budget.
You visited every room. Great job, junior astronaut!
It's getting dark. Look up, can you spot Earth? It's the tiny blue dot!
New Sol! Let's read today's space report together.
Now go to the Energy Panel in the Control Room and share all the available energy.
Systems on! Follow the yellow arrow to your tasks.
Alert! Energetic particles! Run to the Magnetic Shield refuge!
Alert! A CME may hit Mars! Let's go to the Shelter.
Alert! A strong solar flare! Let's be safe in the Shelter.
The Sun is active, but this storm should not reach Mars. Phew!
We're safe in the Shelter. Great running!
Good try! We learn every time.
Great planning! The base is happy.
Oops, some systems needed more energy. Let's plan better next Sol.
Plan the energy first at the Control Room.
Sol {{n}} uses data captured on Earth date {{date}}. This pairing is a story choice: an Earth day and a Mars Sol are not the same length.

Tap the flares from weakest to strongest.
Each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. X flares can go beyond X10!
Drag to today's CME speed to see when it would reach Mars.

WSA+Enlil forecast: no impact on Mars.

Reach the Magnetic Shield refuge before time runs out!

Recovery complete. Base systems are returning to normal.

Trigger: {{wind}}. This is a game simulation, not a NASA dust measurement or a solar flare.
Dust is covering the arrays. Inspect and clean the most-soiled group first to protect the next Sol's energy.
You gave the shield {{allocated}} kWh; it needed {{demand}} kWh, leaving {{missing}} kWh missing. Solar reading: {{flare}}.
Electronics flicker and crew dose rises by {{dose}} game units. Shelter timeout penalty: {{penalty}}. Integrity effect: {{integrity}}.
Life Support received {{allocated}} of {{demand}} kWh. InSight AT mean: {{temp}} °C; colder air increases the existing heat demand.
Life Support received {{allocated}} of {{demand}} kWh. No AT reading was available, so the labeled game fallback set demand.
Cold cabins and frost slow oxygen generation. Oxygen effect: {{oxygen}}.
The Greenhouse received {{allocated}} of {{demand}} kWh, leaving {{missing}} kWh missing.
Leaves droop, grow lights dim and oxygen contribution falls. Oxygen effect: {{oxygen}}.
Simulated storm wind: {{wind}}. Average array dust is now {{dust}}%.
Next Sol's energy pool loses {{loss}}%, capped at 20%. This is a game rule, not measured dust opacity.
Every array was inspected and cleaned in priority order. Remaining average dust: {{dust}}%.
The panels shine again. Next Sol's dust loss is {{loss}}%.
A system received more energy than it needed. Surplus never adds dose or reserves.
The gentle venting glow is harmless, but that energy could help another system.
Every system is in its ideal energy band and the crew completed the plan.
Warm lights, ripe apples and {{integrity}} Integrity / {{oxygen}} Oxygen regeneration, using the existing task reward.
The base needs help. Let's train again!
The crew evacuated safely. No one was hurt on screen; use the cause below to train again.
The crew dose reached 100 game units. The shield needed more energy or the crew missed shelter.
Oxygen reached zero. Life Support and the Greenhouse did not receive enough energy.
Integrity reached zero after the Magnetic Shield deficit. The crew evacuated before further danger.
{{name}} kept Base ARES safe for 5 Sols!
Your nickname stays only on this device.
Sol {{sol}}: the Sun is busy today!
A CME is traveling at {{v}} km/s.
A CME left the Sun at {{v}} km/s, but it should not reach Mars.
Let's hurry to the Magnetic Shield refuge!
A simulated dust storm is using the {{v}} trigger; clean the arrays before sealing.
The shield received {{a}} kWh but needed {{d}}, so dose rose {{dose}} game units.
Life Support received {{a}} of {{d}} kWh, leaving the cabin cold.
The Greenhouse received {{a}} of {{d}} kWh, so growth and oxygen slowed.
Simulated dust reduces the next energy pool by {{loss}}%.
The cleaned arrays restored future solar output.
Hint: today the {{system}} needs the most energy. Look at the report!
Great planning, every system was happy!
The ideal plan was Shield {{s}}, Life Support {{l}} and Greenhouse {{g}} kWh.
A solar flare is a super bright flash on the Sun. Scientists sort them by letters: each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before!
Some space storms send fast tiny particles. The shelter has thick walls that keep astronauts safe until it is over.
The colder it is outside, the faster our base loses heat. So the heaters need more energy to keep us cozy!
Why do I need a shelter?
Why does cold use more energy?

A window into the Universe, recorded by scientists and photographers.

APOD shares astronomy pictures. The NASA library collects images from space missions. Picture dates belong to Earth, not to our game’s Sol clock.
